author: A Robot
objectives: Students will identify and name the four chambers of the heart, the four heart valves, and the major vessels entering and leaving the heart.
Students will trace the path of blood through the heart's dual circulation, naming each chamber, valve, and vessel in order.
Students will distinguish the pulmonary circuit from the systemic circuit and explain why the right and left sides of the heart serve different circulatory functions.

Students will explain why the left ventricle has a substantially thicker myocardium than the right ventricle, relating wall thickness to the pressure required to perfuse the systemic versus pulmonary circuits.
Students will describe the function of the atrioventricular and semilunar valves in preventing backflow, and identify which valves separate which chambers or chamber-vessel pairs.

modules.description: Students are introduced to the gross anatomy of the heart with two side-by-side models: an intact exterior view and an anterior cutaway view. Narration orients students to anatomical left/right conventions.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the anatomical orientation of the heart in the body.
Distinguish the patient's anatomical left and right from the viewer's perspective.
Recognize the major external vessels entering and leaving the heart.
instructions: Observe the two heart models that appear before you.
Use the rotation control to spin both models and examine them from all angles.
Follow the narration to understand anatomical orientation conventions.

components.text: Intact Heart (Exterior)
Cutaway Heart (Anterior Wall Removed)
⚠ Anatomical orientation: labels reflect the PATIENT'S left and right, not the viewer's.
Superior Vena Cava
Inferior Vena Cava
Aorta
Pulmonary Trunk
Pulmonary Veins

clips.changeMeaning: Both heart models appear in the workspace, establishing the initial scene with titles visible above each model.
clips.narration: Welcome to the Heart Anatomy and Circulation lab. Before you, two heart models have appeared. On your left is the intact exterior heart, showing the surface and all major vessels. On your right is a cutaway view with the anterior wall removed, exposing the interior. Both models are life-sized for a human adult heart.

clips.changeMeaning: An orientation warning label appears below both models to remind students that anatomical left/right is from the patient's perspective, not the viewer's.
clips.narration: Before we explore the structures, let's establish orientation. In anatomy, we always describe the heart from the patient's own perspective — so the heart's right side is on YOUR left as you face the patient, and vice versa. Keep this in mind throughout the lab.

clips.changeMeaning: Vessel labels appear on the exterior heart model, identifying all five major vessel groups so students can map external anatomy.
clips.narration: Look at the intact heart on your left. You can see the large vessels entering and leaving at the top and back. The Superior Vena Cava and Inferior Vena Cava enter the right side — they carry blood returning from the body. The Aorta arches upward from the left side, and the Pulmonary Trunk exits toward the lungs. The Pulmonary Veins enter from behind on the left side.

clips.changeMeaning: Both heart models begin slowly auto-rotating so students can see all angles, reinforcing 3D spatial understanding of the organ's orientation.
clips.narration: Take a moment to rotate both heart models. Notice the apex — the pointed inferior tip — is angled slightly to the left. This is its natural position in the chest. The base, where the major vessels emerge, faces superiorly and posteriorly. When you're ready, advance to the next scene for a detailed structural tour.

modules.description: A narrated, label-by-label tour of the four chambers, four valves, and major vessels using the cutaway heart. Each structure is highlighted and labeled in sequence.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Name and locate the four chambers: right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, left ventricle.
Name and locate the four valves: tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral/bicuspid, aortic.
Identify the major vessels: superior and inferior vena cava, pulmonary arteries, pulmonary veins, and aorta.
Map interior structures to external landmarks on the intact heart.
instructions: Follow the narration as each structure is highlighted on the cutaway heart.
Observe how the corresponding region on the intact heart is also highlighted.
Pay attention to the dual name of the mitral/bicuspid valve.

components.text: Structural Tour

clips.changeMeaning: The large cutaway heart and smaller exterior reference heart appear together, and the tour section header is visible. Scene is set for the structural walkthrough.
clips.narration: In this scene we'll take a systematic tour of every named structure inside the heart. We'll start with the four chambers, move to the four valves, and finish with the major vessels. As each structure is highlighted on the cutaway view, watch for the matching highlight on the smaller intact heart to the right — this helps you connect interior anatomy to exterior landmarks.

components.text:
Right Atrium
Thin-walled receiving chamber
Receives: Superior & Inferior Vena Cava

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight ring moves to the right atrium position on the cutaway heart, and the structure label updates to 'Right Atrium — thin-walled receiving chamber'. The exterior heart also shows a corresponding highlight.
clips.narration: The Right Atrium is the first chamber blood enters when returning from the body. It is a thin-walled receiving chamber on the anatomical right side of the heart, forming the right border. The superior and inferior vena cava empty directly into it.

components.text:
Right Ventricle
Moderately thick wall
Pumps to: Lungs (low pressure)

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight moves to right ventricle position; structure label updates to 'Right Ventricle' with functional note about moderate wall thickness.
clips.narration: Below the right atrium is the Right Ventricle. It forms most of the anterior surface of the heart. Its walls are moderately thick — thicker than the atria, but much thinner than the left ventricle — because it only needs to pump blood the short distance to the lungs.

components.text:
Left Atrium
Thin-walled receiving chamber
Receives: 4 Pulmonary Veins

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight moves to left atrium; structure label updates with pulmonary vein connection detail.
clips.narration: The Left Atrium sits on the posterior surface of the heart and receives oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins — four vessels returning from the lungs. Like the right atrium, it is thin-walled; its job is simply to receive and hold blood briefly before passing it to the left ventricle.

components.text:
Left Ventricle
Thick wall (10–15 mm)
Pumps to: Entire body (high pressure)

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight moves to left ventricle; label updates emphasizing thick wall and high-pressure systemic output.
clips.narration: The Left Ventricle is the powerhouse of the heart. It occupies the apex region and forms the left lateral border. Its thick myocardium — roughly 10 to 15 millimeters in a healthy adult — generates the high pressure needed to push blood through the entire systemic circulation.

components.text:
Tricuspid Valve
Atrioventricular (AV) Valve
Right Atrium → Right Ventricle
3 cusps

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight shifts to the tricuspid valve position; label updates to show valve type, location, and cusp count.
clips.narration: Now the valves. The Tricuspid Valve sits between the right atrium and right ventricle. It has three leaf-like cusps — hence 'tri-cuspid.' It is an atrioventricular valve, meaning it separates an atrium from a ventricle. When the ventricle contracts, this valve snaps shut to prevent blood from flowing backward into the right atrium.

components.text:
Pulmonary (Pulmonic) Valve
Semilunar Valve
Right Ventricle → Pulmonary Trunk
3 half-moon cusps

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight moves to pulmonary valve at top of right ventricle; label updates to show semilunar type and location.
clips.narration: The Pulmonary Valve — also called the pulmonic valve — sits at the outflow of the right ventricle where it meets the pulmonary trunk. It is a semilunar valve, named for its three half-moon–shaped cusps. It prevents blood from falling back into the right ventricle after each contraction.

components.text:
Mitral Valve (= Bicuspid Valve)
Atrioventricular (AV) Valve
Left Atrium → Left Ventricle
2 cusps — both names are correct!

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight moves to mitral valve; label emphasizes both clinical names and its two cusps, a common exam distinction.
clips.narration: The Mitral Valve, also known as the Bicuspid Valve, separates the left atrium from the left ventricle. You will encounter both names in clinical practice — 'mitral' is more common clinically, while 'bicuspid' describes its anatomy: it has only two cusps. It is the most forcefully stressed AV valve because the left ventricle generates high pressure.

components.text:
Aortic Valve
Semilunar Valve
Left Ventricle → Aorta
3 half-moon cusps

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight moves to aortic valve position; label updates showing its semilunar nature and position at left ventricle/aorta junction.
clips.narration: The Aortic Valve is the final valve blood passes through before leaving the heart entirely. It sits at the outflow of the left ventricle where it meets the aorta. Like the pulmonary valve it is semilunar with three cusps, and it prevents the high-pressure aortic blood from regurgitating back into the left ventricle during relaxation.

components.text:
Major Vessels
• Sup. Vena Cava — body (upper) → R. Atrium
• Inf. Vena Cava — body (lower) → R. Atrium
• Pulmonary Arteries — R. Ventricle → Lungs
• Pulmonary Veins — Lungs → L. Atrium
• Aorta — L. Ventricle → Body

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight turns off and a comprehensive vessels summary label appears, listing all five vessel groups with their roles to consolidate the structural tour.
clips.narration: Finally, the major vessels. Blood from the upper body returns via the Superior Vena Cava; from the lower body via the Inferior Vena Cava. The Pulmonary Arteries carry deoxygenated blood to the lungs. The Pulmonary Veins return oxygenated blood to the left atrium. The Aorta, the largest artery in the body, distributes oxygenated blood to the systemic circulation.

modules.description: The cutaway heart fills with color-coded blood flow: blue for deoxygenated (right side and pulmonary arteries) and red for oxygenated (left side and pulmonary veins). Labels identify the pulmonary and systemic circuits.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Distinguish oxygenated (red) from deoxygenated (blue) blood by location in the heart.
Identify which side of the heart belongs to the pulmonary circuit and which to the systemic circuit.
Explain the continuous, simultaneous nature of dual-circuit circulation.
instructions: Watch as the heart fills with color-coded blood.
Blue = deoxygenated; Red = oxygenated.
Observe the pulmonary and systemic circuit labels as each is highlighted in turn.

components.sciptDescription: Smoothly pulses the alpha transparency of the object's material between a minimum and maximum value at a configurable pulse rate (pulses per second). Inputs: float minAlpha (0-1), float maxAlpha (0-1), float pulseRate (pulses per second).

Smoothly pulses the alpha transparency of the object's material between a minimum and maximum value at a configurable pulse rate (pulses per second). Inputs: float minAlpha (0-1), float maxAlpha (0-1), float pulseRate (pulses per second).

components.text:
🔵 Deoxygenated Blood
Right side, Pulmonary Arteries,
Systemic Veins

🔴 Oxygenated Blood
Left side, Pulmonary Veins,
Systemic Arteries

⬆  PULMONARY CIRCUIT  ⬆
Right Heart → Lungs → Left Heart

⬇  SYSTEMIC CIRCUIT  ⬇
Left Heart → Body → Right Heart

clips.changeMeaning: Both colored blood flow overlays appear on their respective sides of the cutaway heart, along with the color legend labels, visualizing the simultaneous dual circulation.
clips.narration: The heart actually drives two separate loops of circulation simultaneously. Watch as the heart fills with color. Blue represents deoxygenated blood on the right side; red represents oxygenated blood on the left side. Both sides pump at the same time — the right side feeds the lungs while the left side feeds the rest of the body.

clips.changeMeaning: The pulmonary circuit label appears above the heart, highlighted, drawing student attention to the right-heart-to-lungs-to-left-heart pathway.
clips.narration: This upper loop is the Pulmonary Circuit. Deoxygenated blood leaves the right ventricle through the pulmonary arteries and travels to the lungs, where carbon dioxide is released and oxygen is absorbed. The newly oxygenated blood then returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium. This is a short, low-pressure loop.

clips.changeMeaning: The systemic circuit label appears below the heart, while the pulmonary circuit label dims slightly, distinguishing the two loops spatially.
clips.narration: This lower loop is the Systemic Circuit. Oxygenated blood leaves the left ventricle through the aorta and travels to every tissue in the body — the brain, muscles, organs, and limbs. After delivering oxygen, the now-deoxygenated blood returns through the venae cavae to the right atrium, completing the loop.

clips.changeMeaning: Both circuit labels brighten equally; the color legends pulse to emphasize the counter-intuitive relationship between vessel type and oxygen content — a critical teaching moment.
clips.narration: Here is the key insight: the pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood, and the pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood. This is the opposite of every other artery-vein pair in the body. Arteries always carry blood AWAY from the heart; veins always carry blood TOWARD the heart — regardless of oxygen content. Don't let the colors fool you.

modules.moduleName: Scene 4: Red Blood Cell Step-by-Step Trace
modules.description: A single red blood cell travels through the complete circulatory path one step at a time. Students advance through each step, with narration and labels describing each chamber, valve, and vessel encountered.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Recite the complete ordered sequence of structures a red blood cell passes through in one full circulatory loop.
Identify the point at which the blood cell becomes oxygenated (lung capillaries) and deoxygenated (systemic tissues).
Connect each valve encounter to its anatomical name and position.
instructions: Press 'Next' to advance the red blood cell one step through the circulation.
Read the structure label that appears at each step.
Watch for the color change at the lung capillaries.
You can replay the trace as many times as you like.

components.sciptDescription: Moves a red blood cell object along a predefined list of waypoints one step at a time. Each step is triggered externally via a public method AdvanceStep(). At each waypoint the script updates the cell's position (with a smooth lerp animation), updates the cell's color (input: List of Color per waypoint), enables/disables a companion label object (input: reference to TextMeshPro label GameObject), and sets the label text from a list of strings (input: List<string> structureNames). Inputs: List<Vector3> waypoints, List<Color> waypointColors, List<string> structureLabels, float moveSpeed, GameObject labelObject.

components.text:
START: Superior Vena Cava
Carrying deoxygenated blood
from the upper body
Step 1 of 14 — Press Next to advance

Lung Capillaries
O₂ absorbed / CO₂ released
🔵 → 🔴 Cell becomes oxygenated!

clips.changeMeaning: The cutaway heart and RBC appear at the starting position in the superior vena cava, with the step counter at Step 1 of 14 and the initial structure label visible.
clips.narration: We will now trace a single red blood cell through the complete circulatory loop. The cell starts in the Superior Vena Cava, carrying deoxygenated blood from the upper body. Press Next to advance the cell one step at a time. Watch the label panel on the right for the name of each structure, and watch the cell itself change color as it passes through the lungs.

components.text: Steps 2–6: Right Heart → Pulmonary Arteries

Right Atrium → Tricuspid Valve → Right Ventricle → Pulmonary Valve → Pulmonary Arteries

Blood is still DEOXYGENATED (blue)

clips.changeMeaning: The RBC animates through right atrium, tricuspid valve, right ventricle, pulmonary valve, and pulmonary trunk positions; the step counter and structure label update at each position.
clips.narration: The cell enters the Right Atrium, where deoxygenated blood pools briefly. The atrium contracts, and the Tricuspid Valve swings open, allowing the cell to pass into the Right Ventricle. The ventricle fills, then powerfully contracts. The Pulmonary Valve opens, and the cell shoots into the Pulmonary Trunk and then the Pulmonary Arteries, racing toward the lungs.

components.text: Step 7: Lung Capillaries — Gas Exchange!

Lung Capillaries

CO₂ exits blood → breathed out
O₂ enters blood → from inhaled air

🔵 DEOXYGENATED → 🔴 OXYGENATED

clips.changeMeaning: The lung capillary zone overlay appears; the RBC color changes from blue to red to represent oxygenation — the visual highlight of the entire trace.
clips.narration: The cell arrives at the Lung Capillaries. Here, in the tiny air sacs of the lungs, a remarkable exchange occurs: carbon dioxide diffuses out of the blood and oxygen diffuses in. Watch the cell transform from blue to red as it becomes oxygenated. This gas exchange is the entire purpose of the pulmonary circuit.

components.text: Steps 8–14: Left Heart → Aorta → Body

Pulmonary Veins → Left Atrium → Mitral Valve → Left Ventricle → Aortic Valve → Aorta

Blood is now OXYGENATED (red)

clips.changeMeaning: The RBC (now red) moves through pulmonary veins, left atrium, mitral valve, left ventricle, aortic valve, and aorta; the lung capillary overlay hides; labels update for the left heart journey.
clips.narration: Now oxygenated, the cell travels back through the Pulmonary Veins into the Left Atrium. The mitral valve opens and it passes into the Left Ventricle — the most powerful chamber. The left ventricle contracts forcefully, opening the Aortic Valve and launching the cell into the Aorta and out to the entire body. The loop is complete when the cell returns deoxygenated through the venae cavae.

modules.description: A side-by-side cross-section through both ventricles illustrates the dramatically different wall thicknesses of the right and left ventricles, with scale markers and narration explaining the pressure-based functional rationale.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Visually compare right and left ventricular wall thickness.
Quantify typical healthy wall thickness values (3–5 mm right; 10–15 mm left).
Explain the physiological basis for the thickness difference in terms of systemic versus pulmonary pressure requirements.
instructions: Compare the two ventricular cross-sections side by side.
Read the scale markers on each to understand the thickness difference.
Rotate each model if desired to examine the wall from all angles.

components.text: Right Ventricle
Left Ventricle

Wall thickness:
~3–5 mm
(Low-pressure
pulmonary circuit)

Wall thickness:
~10–15 mm
(High-pressure
systemic circuit)
≈ 3:1 thickness ratio  |  Left ventricle generates ~5× more pressure than right

clips.changeMeaning: The two ventricular cross-section models appear side by side with their header labels, setting up the visual comparison before detailed measurements are introduced.
clips.narration: This scene focuses on one of the most clinically important structural differences in the heart: the asymmetric wall thickness of the two ventricles. Before you are two horizontal cross-sections cut at the same level through the ventricles. The crescent-shaped right ventricle is on your left; the circular, thick-walled left ventricle is on your right.

clips.changeMeaning: Scale marker and thickness label appear on the right ventricle, with blue color emphasis on the RV cross-section to draw attention to its thin wall measurement.
clips.narration: Look at the right ventricle. Its wall is relatively thin — in a healthy adult, approximately 3 to 5 millimeters. The scale marker beside it confirms this. The thin wall is appropriate for the right ventricle's job: it needs only enough pressure to push blood through the short, low-resistance pulmonary circuit to the lungs.

clips.changeMeaning: Scale marker and thickness label appear on the left ventricle with red color emphasis; the visual contrast with the thinner RV immediately communicates the 3:1 ratio.
clips.narration: Now look at the left ventricle. Its wall is dramatically thicker — approximately 10 to 15 millimeters, roughly three times the right ventricle. The left ventricle must generate enough pressure to drive blood through the entire systemic circulation — including the arms, legs, abdominal organs, and crucially, up to the brain against gravity. That takes enormous muscular force.

clips.changeMeaning: The 3:1 ratio annotation label appears at the bottom of the scene, anchoring the numerical relationship; both cross-sections are now fully labeled for student comparison.
clips.narration: This three-to-one thickness ratio, and the five-to-one pressure difference it generates, explains several clinical phenomena. Left ventricular hypertrophy — an abnormal thickening of the left ventricle wall beyond 15 millimeters — is a common consequence of chronic high blood pressure, because the muscle adapts to the extra workload. This is why controlling hypertension protects the heart.

modules.moduleName: Scene 6: Valve Function and Backflow Prevention
modules.description: The four heart valves are examined individually in open and closed states. Students learn the two valve categories (atrioventricular and semilunar) and understand how each prevents backflow during the cardiac cycle.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Categorize the four valves as atrioventricular or semilunar.
Describe which structures each valve separates.
Explain which valves are open and which are closed during ventricular systole versus diastole.
Identify the structural mechanism by which each valve prevents backflow.
instructions: Observe each valve in its open and closed states.
Read the label describing what the valve is doing at each phase.
Follow the narration to understand the cardiac cycle timing.

components.text:
Valve categories:

🟡 AV Valves (between atria & ventricles)
   • Tricuspid (Right)
   • Mitral/Bicuspid (Left)

🟡 Semilunar Valves (ventricle outflows)
   • Pulmonary
   • Aortic
Valve Function — Preventing Backflow

clips.changeMeaning: The cutaway heart appears with the valve category legend on the right side. No individual valve models are shown yet — this sets up the categorical framework.
clips.narration: The heart has four valves divided into two functional categories. The Atrioventricular, or AV, valves sit between the atria and ventricles — the tricuspid on the right, the mitral on the left. The Semilunar valves sit at the outflows of the ventricles — the pulmonary valve on the right, the aortic valve on the left. All four valves work passively — pushed open by blood pressure and slammed shut when pressure reverses.

components.text:
VENTRICULAR SYSTOLE (Contraction)
AV Valves: CLOSED 🔴 | Semilunar Valves: OPEN 🟡

Systole logic:

Ventricle pressure > Atrial pressure
→ AV valves forced SHUT
   (prevents backflow into atria)

Ventricle pressure > Arterial pressure
→ Semilunar valves forced OPEN
   (blood flows into arteries)

clips.changeMeaning: During systole: AV valves (tricuspid and mitral) appear in closed state; semilunar valves (pulmonary and aortic) appear in open state. Phase label updates.
clips.narration: During Ventricular Systole — when the ventricles contract — pressure inside shoots up. This forces the AV valves shut, preventing blood from surging backward into the atria. Simultaneously, the rising pressure forces the Semilunar valves open, launching blood into the pulmonary trunk and aorta. This is the 'lub' of the heart sound.

components.text:
VENTRICULAR DIASTOLE (Relaxation / Filling)
AV Valves: OPEN 🟡 | Semilunar Valves: CLOSED 🔴

Diastole logic:

Arterial pressure > Ventricle pressure
→ Semilunar valves forced SHUT
   (prevents backflow into ventricles)

Atrial pressure > Ventricle pressure
→ AV valves pushed OPEN
   (ventricles refill from atria)

clips.changeMeaning: Valve states swap: semilunar valves switch to closed; AV valves switch to open. Phase label updates to diastole, reinforcing the inverse relationship.
clips.narration: During Ventricular Diastole — when the ventricles relax and refill — the pressure drops. Blood in the aorta and pulmonary trunk is at higher pressure than the relaxed ventricles, so it tries to fall back. This fills the cup-like pockets of the Semilunar valves and snaps them shut. Meanwhile, atrial pressure is now higher than ventricular pressure, pushing the AV valves open so the ventricles can refill. This is the 'dub' of the heart sound.

components.text:
A unit of blood has just entered the RIGHT ATRIUM.
What is the NEXT structure it will pass through?
A) Mitral Valve
B) Tricuspid Valve
C) Pulmonary Valve
D) Aortic Valve
Flow Quiz — Step 1 of 14

clips.changeMeaning: The heart appears with the first highlight on the right atrium and the first scenario question displayed, buttons populated with choices for the first step of the flow quiz.

This tests not just memorization but understanding of direction — for example, do you know which way blood flows through each valve? Pay special attention to the pulmonary artery and vein questions — remember, pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood and pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood.

components.text: Lab Recap: Heart Anatomy & Circulation

1. STRUCTURAL INVENTORY
4 Chambers · 4 Valves · 5 Vessel Groups

2. DUAL-CIRCUIT ORGANIZATION
Pulmonary Circuit (right) + Systemic Circuit (left)

3. BLOOD CELL PATHWAY
SVC → R.Atrium → Tricuspid → R.Ventricle → Pulmonary V. → Lungs → Pulm. Veins → L.Atrium → Mitral → L.Ventricle → Aortic V. → Aorta

4. WALL THICKNESS ASYMMETRY
LV (~10–15 mm) ≈ 3× thicker than RV (~3–5 mm)
Due to higher systemic pressure demands

5. VALVE BACKFLOW PREVENTION
AV valves close in systole · Semilunar valves close in diastole

clips.changeMeaning: All five recap cards appear simultaneously alongside the slowly rotating cutaway heart, giving students a full visual overview of the lab's content before detailed review.
clips.narration: Excellent work completing the Heart Anatomy and Circulation lab. Let's review the five concept areas you've explored. Each card summarizes one area; follow along as we highlight each in turn.

clips.changeMeaning: The recap highlight glow moves to card 1 (Structural Inventory), visually emphasizing it while the narration reviews its content.
clips.narration: First: the structural inventory. The heart has four chambers — right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, left ventricle — four valves — tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral or bicuspid, and aortic — and five major vessel connections: the superior vena cava, inferior vena cava, pulmonary arteries, pulmonary veins, and aorta.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight moves to card 2 (Dual-Circuit Organization); card 1 returns to its resting color to de-emphasize it.
clips.narration: Second: dual-circuit organization. The right heart drives the pulmonary circuit — a short, low-pressure loop to the lungs. The left heart drives the systemic circuit — a long, high-pressure loop to the entire body. Both sides beat simultaneously and move equal volumes of blood per beat.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight moves to card 3 (Blood Cell Pathway); card 2 returns to resting color.
clips.narration: Third: the complete blood cell pathway. Starting from the superior vena cava, blood flows through the right atrium, tricuspid valve, right ventricle, pulmonary valve, pulmonary arteries, lung capillaries where it gains oxygen, pulmonary veins, left atrium, mitral valve, left ventricle, aortic valve, and finally out the aorta to the body.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight moves to card 4 (Wall Thickness Asymmetry); card 3 returns to resting color.
clips.narration: Fourth: wall thickness asymmetry. The left ventricle's myocardium is approximately 10 to 15 millimeters thick — roughly three times the right ventricle's 3 to 5 millimeters. This is because the left ventricle must generate far greater pressure to perfuse the systemic circuit. Left ventricular hypertrophy is a key clinical consequence of chronic hypertension.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight moves to card 5 (Valve Backflow Prevention); card 4 returns to resting color, completing the sequential recap.
clips.narration: Fifth: valve backflow prevention. The two atrioventricular valves — tricuspid and mitral — close during ventricular systole to prevent backflow into the atria. The two semilunar valves — pulmonary and aortic — close during ventricular diastole to prevent backflow into the ventricles. Together they ensure one-directional flow through the heart on every beat.

clips.changeMeaning: All five recap cards brighten equally as the highlight fades, and the rotating heart model completes a final turn — a celebratory visual cue marking lab completion.
clips.narration: That concludes the Heart Anatomy and Circulation lab. You can return to any individual scene to review, or replay the quizzes to test your retention. In your upcoming coursework you'll apply these structural foundations to understanding cardiac pathologies, electrocardiography, and the pharmacology of heart medications. Well done, and good luck!
